echoes.note: Paul's self-description 'in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling' (v.3) draws on the stock biblical pairing of fear and trembling, programmatically stated in the Song of the Sea where 'fear and dread' and 'trembling' fall on the nations before God's power. Volume is faint and the idiom is diffuse, but it coheres with Paul's argument that the awe belongs to God's power, not human eloquence. Contested as a specific source.

'Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling' supplies the closest devotional sense of Paul's 'fear and much trembling' (v.3) as the proper posture of a servant before God's power. The verbal overlap is real in the Greek (phobos/tromos) but the phrase is formulaic, so the echo is faint and contested against the wider 'fear and trembling' tradition.

Paul's refusal of 'lofty speech or wisdom' so that faith rests 'in the power of God' (vv.1,5) extends Jeremiah's oracle that the wise must not boast in wisdom but only in knowing the LORD. The theme is carried over from 1 Corinthians 1:31, giving recurrence, but the link here is thematic rather than verbal and so faint.

Paul's 'God's wisdom in a mystery (mysterion), hidden, foreordained before the ages' (vv.7) is steeped in Daniel's Aramaic hymn praising God 'to whom belong wisdom and might,' who 'reveals deep and hidden things.' Daniel is the Septuagintal seedbed for mysterion as divinely hidden-then-revealed knowledge, giving strong coherence with Paul's whole argument; the cluster of wisdom + mystery + revelation supplies recurrence.

'There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries' is arguably the direct conceptual source for Paul's claim that God's once-hidden wisdom is now revealed (vv.7,10). The technical use of mysterion for an eschatological secret disclosed by God is distinctively Danielic, lending high coherence even without verbatim quotation.

Wisdom 'foreordained before the ages for our glory' (v.7) evokes the personified Wisdom of Proverbs 8, possessed by the LORD 'at the beginning of his work, before the earth was.' The pre-cosmic, pre-temporal location of God's wisdom is the shared point; Paul transposes the Wisdom tradition christologically, so this is figural as much as verbal.

Paul's hidden divine wisdom destined for the glory of those who love God parallels the Wisdom of Solomon's portrait of Sophia as a pure emanation of God's glory that passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God. The Second-Temple sapiential matrix (availability secure) gives strong coherence; 'for our glory' (v.7) echoes Wisdom's glory-language.

The motif of a wisdom present with God before the world, inaccessible to human counsel, undergirds Paul's 'wisdom of God in a mystery' that none of the rulers knew (vv.7-8). Wisdom 9 also feeds 2:16 below, giving recurrence across the chapter and strengthening the case for Paul's reliance on this prayer of Solomon.

'They would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (v.8) most plausibly draws its title from the repeated 'the King of glory... the LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory.' The transfer of a divine glory-title to the crucified Christ is figural and striking; volume rests on the rare phrase 'of glory' applied to the Lord.

'The God of glory thunders' offers an alternative scriptural source for Paul's 'Lord of glory' (v.8), part of the same Psalter glory-theophany vocabulary as Psalm 24. The link is faint and overlaps with the stronger Psalm 24 candidate.

Isaiah's vision of the LORD high and lifted up, his glory filling the earth, lies behind the 'Lord of glory' title (v.8) as a theophanic background; rulers who 'did not know' the glory recall Isaiah's commission to a people who see but do not perceive. The connection is thematic and contested against the more verbally exact Psalm 24.

The explicit citation formula 'as it is written' introduces v.9, 'what no eye has seen, nor ear heard...what God has prepared for those who love him,' which most closely matches Isaiah 64:4 (LXX: God acts for those who wait/love him; eye has not seen a God besides you). This is the controlling source-text, though Paul's wording is conflate and not verbatim with any extant version.

'Nor did it enter into the heart of man' (v.9) closely matches Isaiah 65:17 LXX, 'the former things shall not be remembered nor come up into the heart,' suggesting Paul conflated Isaiah 64:4 with the new-creation oracle of Isaiah 65. The shared 'heart' idiom and eschatological 'what God has prepared' give this a strong claim to be part of the quotation's source matrix.

Sirach 1:10, 'he supplied wisdom to those who love him,' has been proposed as a partial source for the closing phrase 'for those who love him' (v.9), since this exact clause is absent from Isaiah. The verbal tie is narrow and the dominant source remains Isaianic, so this is a contested supplementary echo.

'The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God' (v.10) coheres with Daniel's 'he reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness.' Within the same chapter Paul has already leaned on Daniel 2 for mystery-language (recurrence), so the depths/revelation motif here reinforces that dependence.

'The spirit of the man which is in him' knows 'the things of a man' (v.11) draws on Proverbs 20:27, 'the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all the inward parts.' The shared verb 'search' and the human spirit as inner knower make this a strong conceptual source for Paul's analogy between man's spirit and God's Spirit.

'The deep things of God' that only the Spirit can search (v.10) directly answers Zophar's challenge, 'Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty?' Paul affirms what Job's friends deemed impossible, now made possible by the Spirit; the verbal tie to 'deep things of God' is close.

Judith's rebuke, 'you cannot plumb the depth of the human heart...how can you search out God who made all things, or comprehend his mind?' parallels Paul's claim that only the Spirit searches God's depths (vv.10-11) and anticipates 2:16. The Second-Temple availability is secure but the verbal overlap is loose, so the echo is faint.

'The spirit of the man which is in him' (v.11) may glance at Zechariah's description of the LORD who 'forms the spirit of man within him,' grounding the human inner spirit Paul invokes. The link is thematic and faint, overlapping with the stronger Proverbs 20:27 candidate.

Verse 16 'For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?' is a direct quotation of Isaiah 40:13 LXX ('Who has known the mind of the LORD, and who has been his counselor that he should instruct him?'). The wording tracks the Septuagint closely; Paul deploys the unanswerable rhetorical question, then stunningly claims 'we have the mind of Christ.'

Solomon's prayer, 'For who can know the counsel of God?...who has learned your counsel unless you gave wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit?' undergirds both Paul's contrast of the unspiritual person who cannot receive God's things (v.14) and the Isaiah 40:13 citation (v.16). The pairing of the 'who can know God's mind' question with the gift of the Spirit makes Wisdom 9 a likely mediating source; recurrence with 2:6-9 strengthens it.

Eliphaz's taunt, 'Have you listened in the council of God, and do you limit wisdom to yourself?' anticipates the rhetorical thrust of v.16, 'who has known the mind of the Lord?' The motif of inaccessible divine counsel is shared, but the verbal link is to Isaiah rather than Job, so this is a faint, contested background echo.

'Who has stood in the council of the LORD to see and hear his word?' supplies the same prophetic topos of access to the divine mind that Paul invokes in v.16. The thematic coherence with the 'mind of the Lord' question is real but the controlling text is Isaiah 40:13, so this remains a faint supplementary echo.
